item.title: Trump’s Supreme Court defeat comes back to haunt him in $166 billion fight
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that lawyers for more than 330,000 importers asked the U.S. Court of International Trade to order refunds of roughly $166 billion collected through President Donald Trump’s emergency tariffs. The Supreme Court ruled in February that imposing those tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act exceeded Trump’s authority. Customs and Border Protection had refunded more than $115 billion as of August, but thousands of importers—including small business
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that lawyers for more than 330,000 importers asked the U.S. Court of International Trade to order refunds of roughly $166 billion collected through President Donald Trump’s emergency tariffs. The Supreme Court ruled in February that imposing those tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act exceeded Trump’s authority.

Customs and Border Protection had refunded more than $115 billion as of August, but thousands of importers—including small businesses and individual online buyers—were still waiting. Judge Richard Eaton ruled in March that every importer who paid the unlawful tariffs was entitled to repayment and issued a universal refund order in April. The administration appealed in June, arguing that only importers who filed lawsuits should receive refunds and that Eaton exceeded his authority.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The class-action lawyers contend that a court order would give CBP the authority it says it needs to issue complete refunds with interest. The Justice Department faced a Friday deadline to answer the complaint and a December 9 deadline to respond to the requested relief.

The government created the debt

This is not primarily a dispute about paperwork. The executive branch imposed tariffs under authority the Supreme Court later found insufficient, collected the money, and then resisted returning it uniformly.

The institutional power is unmistakable. The administration set the tariff policy. CBP collected the payments. The Justice Department chose to appeal the order covering all affected importers. Businesses and consumers did not create this legal disorder; they absorbed its costs.

Rights for those who can afford them

The administration’s preferred remedy would divide people with the same entitlement into two classes: those able to sue the federal government and those unable to do so. That is not a neutral administrative distinction. It makes access to lawyers, documents and litigation money determine whether the government must return funds it was not authorized to collect.

The class action exists because more than 330,000 importers should not need 330,000 separate legal fights to enforce one ruling about one federal policy. A remedy limited to successful plaintiffs would convert an unlawful exaction into a litigation surcharge on smaller businesses.

Procedure as misdirection

The administration says CBP cannot issue refunds without a court order. Yet it appealed the universal order that purported to supply that authority. Whatever the ultimate jurisdictional ruling, the practical effect of that position is clear: the government invokes procedural limits while contesting the procedure that could deliver broad repayment.

That contradiction is the story’s center. Focusing on technical problems, missing paperwork or the difficulties faced by third-party buyers risks shifting attention toward weaker actors navigating the aftermath. Those complications matter, but they followed an executive decision that the Supreme Court rejected.

The cost moved downward

Tariffs are collected from importers, not from foreign governments. According to the reporting, affected companies raised prices amid the tariff policy and the war with Iran; refunds could relieve some of that pressure and make consumer reimbursements more likely.

The administration therefore controlled the policy while businesses and buyers carried the immediate burden. Its effort to restrict repayment would preserve that asymmetry even after the underlying exercise of power failed in court. The state acted broadly when collecting the money and now argues for narrowness when returning it.

Executive maximalism, remedial minimalism

The larger pattern is government by expansive assertion followed by cramped accountability. Executive authority is treated as capacious when officials want to impose costs, then suddenly constrained when courts require relief.

The Supreme Court defeat did not itself make repayment automatic, because institutions still decide whether a ruling becomes a remedy in practice. That is where power hides after the headline: in appeals, administrative bottlenecks and rules that make injured parties spend more money to recover what the government should not have taken.

item.title: Retired general 'couldn’t be prouder' after Hegseth earned soldier’s rebuke
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that retired Brig. Gen. Ty Seidule praised an Old Guard soldier who ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s group to remain quiet at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Seidule told Democratic strategist James Carville that the soldier “did exactly what he was supposed to do” by enforcing the required silence and respect. Their Veterans Day discussion also addressed Donald Trump’s proposed giant arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Seidule cited Washington Post rep
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that retired Brig. Gen. Ty Seidule praised an Old Guard soldier who ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s group to remain quiet at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Seidule told Democratic strategist James Carville that the soldier “did exactly what he was supposed to do” by enforcing the required silence and respect.

Their Veterans Day discussion also addressed Donald Trump’s proposed giant arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Seidule cited Washington Post reporting that the structure would obstruct established sight lines, including the view of John F. Kennedy’s grave, prompting the Kennedy family to sue.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Authority met discipline

Hegseth holds institutional power over the Defense Department. The soldier does not. Yet at the Tomb, the soldier had a defined duty: protect the ceremony’s silence and dignity, regardless of the visitor’s rank.

That distinction matters. The correction was not insubordination or personal confrontation. It was a service member applying a rule to a powerful civilian official. Seidule’s approval recognizes something increasingly scarce in political institutions: duty that does not dissolve when authority becomes inconvenient.

The rebuke was earned

The headline’s retired general is Seidule, and the conduct he celebrated was the soldier’s refusal to grant Hegseth an exemption from the standards imposed on everyone else.

Carville asked whether the soldier might receive a dressing-down. That possibility exposes the real power imbalance. Hegseth could face a moment of public embarrassment; the soldier could face consequences inside the hierarchy Hegseth leads. The meaningful act was not merely requesting quiet. It was enforcing institutional standards upward.

Seidule sharpened the indictment by naming the Tomb guard’s principles—silence, respect, dignity and perseverance—and saying they are qualities the defense secretary lacks. That is political criticism grounded in conduct, not ceremonial pageantry.

Arlington is not a backdrop

The proposed arch raises the same underlying question at a larger scale: whether powerful officials treat Arlington as a national cemetery with its own history or as scenery available for their preferred monument.

According to the reporting Seidule cited, the arch would interfere with carefully established views among Arlington’s memorial sites. Its size is therefore not an aesthetic footnote. A monument that dominates the cemetery’s visual landscape also asserts control over how the place is seen and remembered.

The misdirection would be to reduce opposition to taste or family sensitivity. The decision-making power rests with those advancing a structure capable of overriding the existing landscape. The Kennedy family’s reported lawsuit is a response to that exercise of power, not its cause.

Standards only matter upward

The soldier’s command and the arch dispute reveal the same political pattern. Institutions are praised for discipline, sacrifice and continuity until those values obstruct an official’s behavior or ambition. Then the people defending the institution risk being recast as the problem.

Arlington’s guards maintain exacting rituals through severe weather because the ceremony is not supposed to bend around individual importance. A government that celebrates such discipline while expecting exceptions for its leaders is not honoring military tradition. It is using that tradition as decoration.

Power wants the ceremony without the constraint

The larger conflict is between stewardship and possession. The Old Guard treats the Tomb as something entrusted to it. Political power too often treats public institutions and memorial spaces as assets to command.

One soldier’s correction briefly reversed that arrangement: the official with greater power was subject to the rule. That is why the incident resonates beyond etiquette. Institutions survive only when their standards bind the people at the top—and when those tasked with enforcing them are not punished for doing their jobs.

item.title: Reporter pulls back curtain on Trump 'game plan' as he fumes in White House
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s White House plans to fight congressional subpoenas after Democrats won control of Congress and announced investigations into his administration and family. CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins described the strategy as more combative than Trump’s first-term resistance to congressional oversight, with Attorney General Todd Blanche reinforcing that position publicly and in a letter to incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia. The investigation
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s White House plans to fight congressional subpoenas after Democrats won control of Congress and announced investigations into his administration and family. CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins described the strategy as more combative than Trump’s first-term resistance to congressional oversight, with Attorney General Todd Blanche reinforcing that position publicly and in a letter to incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia.

The investigations described by AlterNet concern alleged self-enrichment and other possible wrongdoing. Conservative commentator Bill O’Reilly urged Trump to explain the Trump family’s financial conduct before investigators define the issue for him, but Collins reported that Trump instead grew increasingly angry after the midterms and prepared for confrontation.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Garcia said officials could answer questions before Congress or face scrutiny later, potentially in state courts. The report does not establish how Democrats would overcome executive-privilege claims or prolonged litigation.

The power sits in the executive branch

This is not a clash between equally situated partisans trading insults. The White House controls executive agencies, records and officials whose testimony Congress may seek. Congress possesses subpoena and investigative authority, but enforcement can become a grinding court battle when an administration refuses cooperation.

Trump made the central choice reported here: resistance rather than disclosure. Blanche then used the authority of the Justice Department to reinforce that posture. Whatever legal arguments eventually emerge, the political strategy is already visible—make oversight expensive, slow and institutionally exhausting.

Obstruction as a governing method

O’Reilly’s advice was tactical, not ethical: explain the family’s conduct before congressional investigators seize the initiative. Trump’s reported answer was escalation.

That distinction matters. The dispute is not merely about an angry president or hostile political coverage. It concerns whether executive power can be used to prevent another branch from examining alleged wrongdoing. Collins’s comparison with Trump’s first term places the current plan within a practiced method: resist subpoenas, assert privilege and force Congress into litigation while time drains from its mandate.

Anger is not an explanation

The article devotes substantial attention to Trump “fuming” after Republican losses. That may describe his mood, but mood is not agency. Anger did not write Blanche’s letter, formulate the executive-privilege claims or decide that subpoenas should be fought.

Personalizing institutional defiance as presidential temper risks turning a calculated use of government power into another episode of Trump psychodrama. The consequential fact is not that he disliked the election coverage. It is that his administration reportedly intends to convert that hostility into an official policy of noncooperation.

Accountability has a clock

Garcia’s warning about future prosecution projects confidence, but it also exposes Congress’s weakness. A subpoena delayed through litigation can become functionally useless even if Congress ultimately prevails. Elections change committee leadership, legislative terms expire and public attention moves on.

His reference to possible state proceedings acknowledges that congressional oversight and criminal prosecution are different mechanisms. Congress can investigate and expose; prosecutors decide whether evidence supports charges. Threatening later vulnerability cannot substitute for an enforceable plan to obtain testimony and records now.

The system rewards delay

The larger pattern is institutional, not temperamental. Executive officials can exploit legal process itself as a shield, betting that delay will outlast the investigators seeking answers. Congress may hold formal authority while lacking a fast, reliable means to enforce it.

That imbalance turns oversight into a contest of endurance. The administration holds the information, commands the agencies and benefits from every month of litigation. Unless congressional power can operate on a political timetable, defiance is not merely resistance. It becomes a successful governing strategy.

item.title: Nobel economist unmasks 'betrayal at the highest levels' in Trump’s orbit
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that economist Paul Krugman called the handling of a national-security inquiry involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang evidence of “betrayal at the highest levels” around President Donald Trump. Huang acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects of spying for Beijing. According to The New York Times account cited by AlterNet, Commerce Department agents investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chip
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that economist Paul Krugman called the handling of a national-security inquiry involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang evidence of “betrayal at the highest levels” around President Donald Trump. Huang acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects of spying for Beijing.

According to The New York Times account cited by AlterNet, Commerce Department agents investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China stopped their probe after Nvidia’s top lawyer contacted them, and the Justice Department assumed control of the case. Commerce said proper procedures were followed. Nvidia’s board said it had found no indication that national security was compromised and is investigating. Trump defended Jensen Huang.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Krugman argues that the episode belongs to a broader pattern: an administration weakened by hostility toward expertise, ideological affinity for authoritarian power and financial relationships that can create pressure to protect wealthy benefactors. His claims about favors being exchanged, including those involving Jared Kushner, are expressly predictions rather than established findings.

The power sits above the affair

The affair is the lurid detail, but it is not the institutional event. Huang did not command Commerce agents or the Justice Department. Executive-branch officials did. The consequential question is therefore not merely whether Huang exposed himself to manipulation, but who decided that the investigation should stop at Commerce, why Justice took control and what happened after that transfer.

Commerce says the case was handled by the book. That may describe procedure; it does not resolve the political question of discretion. A powerful company’s lawyer reached investigators, the inquiry changed hands and the president publicly defended the company’s chief executive. Those are reported facts requiring scrutiny without pretending they already prove improper interference.

Access is a form of power

Krugman points to Nvidia’s reported $25 million contribution to Trump’s ballroom and broader financial support flowing from the artificial-intelligence industry toward Trump. AlterNet’s account does not establish a quid pro quo. It does establish the conditions under which the possibility matters: concentrated private wealth, direct access to political leadership and government decisions carrying enormous commercial and national-security consequences.

The relevant standard is not whether a payment can be matched to a written order. A political system is already compromised when officials know that enforcing security rules against a major patron may cost them money, prestige or allegiance. Financial dependence can distort judgment without leaving behind a tidy receipt labeled “favor.”

Loyalty displaces competence

Krugman’s larger charge is that Trump’s political operation treats expertise as a liability because independent knowledge creates independent judgment. His example is Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fixation on testosterone while warfare is being transformed by drones and artificial intelligence.

The pattern is more consequential than individual foolishness. Institutions become fragile when professional competence is subordinated to personal loyalty. Officials selected for obedience are less likely to challenge a president, resist a donor or persist with an inquiry that inconveniences an ally. What looks like administrative confusion can therefore be the predictable output of an administration built to discourage resistance.

The framing can hide the decision-makers

Calling this “the Huang scandal” risks directing attention toward personal recklessness while obscuring the officials who possessed coercive power. Huang’s conduct may have created a security concern. Only government actors could decide how aggressively to investigate it, whether commercial influence received special accommodation and whether the public would receive an accounting.

Krugman goes further than the reported record when he describes moral treason and predicts future revelations of exchanged favors. Those are his interpretations, not findings established by the events AlterNet recounts. The stronger fact-grounded indictment is narrower: wealth and presidential access surrounded a sensitive inquiry, the investigation was transferred after corporate intervention, and the available official assurances leave the exercise of government discretion as the central issue.

Patriotism without sacrifice

This episode reveals the hollowness of nationalism used as branding. The people chanting loudest about national strength face a basic test when security enforcement conflicts with political loyalty, ideological affinity or financial advantage. Krugman’s argument is that Trump’s circle repeatedly chooses the latter.

The systemic danger lies in that incentive structure, regardless of what Nvidia’s board or the government investigation ultimately concludes about espionage. When leaders centralize discretion, disparage expertise and cultivate wealthy patrons, national security becomes selectively enforced. The flag remains onstage; the state’s capacity to act independently is what gets traded away.

item.title: Trump’s morning rant continues with series of rage attacks on GOP and Dems
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump spent more than two hours Thursday morning posting attacks on Democrats and Republicans after GOP losses in the 2026 midterms. He blamed the results on his absence from the ballot, accused Democrats of corruption and cheating without elaborating, revived warnings about migrant “caravans,” and faulted Senate Republicans for preserving the filibuster rather than passing the SAVE Act. Trump also repeated a misleading account of the congress
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump spent more than two hours Thursday morning posting attacks on Democrats and Republicans after GOP losses in the 2026 midterms. He blamed the results on his absence from the ballot, accused Democrats of corruption and cheating without elaborating, revived warnings about migrant “caravans,” and faulted Senate Republicans for preserving the filibuster rather than passing the SAVE Act.

Trump also repeated a misleading account of the congressional effort to obtain his tax returns. He claimed investigators “found nothing,” while the inquiry found that the IRS had largely failed to follow its mandatory presidential-audit policy during his first administration. The returns showed little federal income tax paid in several years and none in 2020, though that alone does not establish fraud.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Later, Trump urged Vice President JD Vance to target Democratic-run cities and states, alleged that billions of dollars were being stolen, and abruptly invoked the Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz. AlterNet reports that he provided no details supporting the sweeping corruption claims quoted in the article.

The power is in the office

This was not merely an aggrieved partisan posting through a bad morning. Trump holds the presidency. Vance holds the vice presidency. Senate Republicans control—or, according to Trump’s own taunt after the reported losses, recently lost—legislative power. When the president tells his deputy to “target” jurisdictions governed by the opposing party, the institutional imbalance matters more than the rant’s disordered presentation.

Democratic governors and city officials are not powerless, but they do not command the federal executive branch. Trump does. Treating his statements chiefly as emotional spectacle risks concealing the relevant fact: a president was publicly identifying rival jurisdictions as appropriate objects of federal attention while offering sweeping criminal accusations against their leaders.

Blame as a loyalty test

Trump assigned responsibility everywhere except to himself. Democrats supposedly cheated. Migrant caravans returned as an electoral warning. Senate Republicans supposedly committed a historic error by refusing to eliminate the filibuster. Voters were told for months to behave as though Trump were on the ballot; after the losses, his absence became the excuse.

That contradiction serves a political function. Trump claims personal ownership of Republican enthusiasm when it produces victories and detaches himself from the party when it loses. Republican officials are reduced to instruments whose competence is measured by whether they convert his demands into law.

His message to John Thune and the remaining GOP senators—congratulations on another year of leadership, “Minority though it may be”—was not analysis. It was discipline by humiliation. Trump was telling Republican officeholders that failure belongs to them, while authority within the party remains his.

Corruption without particulars

Trump’s accusations against “Blue States” were maximal and nonspecific: billions stolen every month, criminality embedded in Democratic leadership, corruption sufficient to balance the federal budget if eliminated. The article reports no explanation for those figures or identification of the alleged theft.

This is accusation used as political infrastructure. The charge does not need to resolve into a case; its purpose is to establish that opposition government is inherently illegitimate. Once that premise is repeated often enough, investigations, funding threats, and selective enforcement can be presented as routine cleanup rather than partisan retaliation.

The tax-return grievance follows the same pattern. Congressional scrutiny becomes persecution, while the documented failure of the IRS to apply its presidential-audit policy recedes from view. Oversight of Trump is cast as corruption; unsupported allegations by Trump are cast as self-evident truth.

The spectacle obscures the program

AlterNet’s emphasis on “rants,” “rage attacks,” and the half-hour rhythm of Trump’s posts captures the behavior but weakens the political frame. Anger is the presentation. The program underneath it is clearer: delegitimize election losses, revive immigration fear, pressure senators to dismantle procedural restraints, discredit oversight, and direct federal suspicion toward opposition-led governments.

Calling this confusion would be a category error. The transitions were erratic, but the distribution of blame was consistent. Trump absolved himself, criminalized Democrats, menaced weaker targets, and punished insufficiently obedient Republicans. Disorder in expression does not mean absence of purpose or consequence.

Government as partisan possession

The larger pattern is the conversion of public authority into a loyalty system. Institutions are legitimate when they protect Trump, elections are credible when his party wins, oversight is lawful when aimed at opponents, and federal power is properly used when it disciplines jurisdictions outside his coalition.

That is the systemic error: coverage can become so absorbed by the president’s temperament that it understates the machinery available to him. The consequential fact is not that Trump posted furiously before breakfast. It is that the person making these accusations controls the executive branch, names political enemies as targets, and pressures his party to remove institutional barriers standing between his grievance and government action.

item.title: Fox ally: Trump needs 'extraordinary legal chops' for inevitable impeachment
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that conservative broadcaster and Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt expects repeated impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth during the next Congress. Hewitt argued that Trump should therefore appoint a press secretary with “extraordinary legal chops”—ideally a recent Supreme Court clerk familiar with expansive theories of presidential power. The White House press secretary position has reportedly remained vacant sinc
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that conservative broadcaster and Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt expects repeated impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth during the next Congress. Hewitt argued that Trump should therefore appoint a press secretary with “extraordinary legal chops”—ideally a recent Supreme Court clerk familiar with expansive theories of presidential power.

The White House press secretary position has reportedly remained vacant since Katie Zacharia departed in mid-October after five days on the job. Meanwhile, the House voted 211–204 to send a Hegseth impeachment resolution to committee, effectively ending that effort for the current Congress.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Hewitt predicted that a future Democratic majority would approve some articles of impeachment but that Senate Republicans would prevent Trump’s removal. His proposed response is not a change in presidential conduct. It is a more legally sophisticated communications operation.

The power is in the votes

Hewitt’s forecast identifies the governing power structure clearly: a House majority can investigate and impeach, but removal requires a two-thirds Senate vote. He expects Democrats to control the first mechanism and Republicans to block the second.

That makes his description of impeachment trials as a “gigantic waste of time” an exercise in partisan framing. Congressional scrutiny does not become inherently pointless because loyal senators are expected to prevent its ultimate sanction. That expectation instead reveals where decisive power lies: with Republican senators willing to insulate the administration from removal.

A lawyer for the message machine

A press secretary does not determine whether presidential conduct is lawful. The job shapes how the White House presents that conduct to journalists and the public. Hewitt’s preferred candidate would combine constitutional expertise with the ability to “battle” the press corps.

That proposal collapses legal defense and public information into one operation. The objective is to give the administration an advocate who can turn disputes over presidential authority into controlled messaging—and who can overwhelm generalist reporters with specialized doctrine. Legal fluency becomes a communications weapon rather than an institutional restraint.

Accountability recast as aggression

Hewitt compares the anticipated press corps to the reporters covering Richard Nixon’s final years and describes future journalists as collectively combative. That framing places scrutiny itself in the defendant’s chair.

The central question is displaced. Instead of asking what conduct might produce impeachment articles, the argument treats impeachment and aggressive reporting as inevitable partisan attacks requiring superior counterprogramming. Possible abuses of power disappear behind a story about hostile Democrats, hostile journalists, and the tactical burden imposed on Trump.

The presidency as permanent defense campaign

The vacancy matters because Hewitt sees the press office as part of an approaching constitutional war. His answer is to recruit someone steeped in Article II doctrine and favorable to broad presidential power, then position that person between the administration and public scrutiny.

That is the larger pattern: institutional accountability is treated not as a constraint to obey, but as an adversary to defeat. Congress investigates, the press questions, lawyers construct the defense, and partisan senators provide the final shield. The system remains formally intact while each mechanism is converted into another front in an organized campaign against consequence.

item.title: The GOP is dying right in front of our eyes
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet argues that the Republican Party is facing possible political collapse after Democrats reportedly won overwhelming victories in the 2026 midterms. The article says Democrats were headed toward an 80-to-90-seat House majority and an eight-to-12-seat Senate majority, gained hundreds of state legislative seats, secured trifectas in 22 states, and won governorships in all 10 traditional presidential battlegrounds. Those results were still being counted when the piece was writt
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet argues that the Republican Party is facing possible political collapse after Democrats reportedly won overwhelming victories in the 2026 midterms. The article says Democrats were headed toward an 80-to-90-seat House majority and an eight-to-12-seat Senate majority, gained hundreds of state legislative seats, secured trifectas in 22 states, and won governorships in all 10 traditional presidential battlegrounds. Those results were still being counted when the piece was written.

The article attributes the Republican defeat largely to Donald Trump and contends that his election-night response—claiming Republicans would have won had he been on the ballot—showed no willingness to change course. It further reports that Trump installed Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff two days later, while House Republicans selected Jim Jordan as their leader.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

From those developments, the author predicts another Republican rout in 2028 and even the party’s possible extinction. But the article also quotes Brookings cautioning that midterm results do not reliably determine the next presidential election.

Power survived the wave

The voters described here imposed a severe electoral penalty. They did not erase Republican power.

Trump still controlled the executive branch at the time of the report. Republicans still held 18 state trifectas. A conservative Supreme Court remained capable of shaping federal policy. State governments, courts, administrative agencies and party institutions do not vanish because one election produces a landslide.

Calling the GOP “dead” confuses defeat with disarmament. A party can lose nationally while retaining enough institutional machinery to obstruct legislation, restrict rights, entrench favorable rules and prepare its return. The article’s victory lap understates the durability of the very power structure it condemns.

Republicans made their choice

The central act of agency was not Trump’s refusal to become reflective. Expecting self-correction from a leader whose public response was to deny responsibility mistakes a repeated political strategy for a personality defect.

Republican officials had choices. According to AlterNet, House Republicans answered the defeat by elevating Jim Jordan, a figure identified with the party’s combative right wing. They continued operating under Trump’s dominance rather than using their institutional authority to break with him. Trump exerted power, but elected Republicans enabled that power because resistance threatened their standing inside the party.

The article sometimes lets them hide behind cowardice. Fear may explain submission; it does not cancel responsibility. These officials are not hostages to Trump. They are political actors who repeatedly decided that his coalition was more valuable than accountability.

Extinction is the wrong frame

The dinosaur metaphor turns politics into natural history, as though parties disappear through evolution rather than organization, money, law and strategic adaptation. Republican decline is not an automatic process. Neither is Democratic ascendancy.

The article’s own historical caveat punctures its forecast: major midterm losses have been followed by presidential victories for the defeated president’s party, while other waves have carried into the next cycle. Declaring that precedent irrelevant does not make it so. A reported Democratic popular-vote margin of 13 points in one midterm cannot, by itself, establish a filibuster-proof Senate or a Democratic presidency two years later.

The same overreach appears in the claim that Texas has effectively entered battleground status. The reported results may justify treating more states as competitive. They do not convert possibility into permanence.

The stronger indictment

The most consequential story is not that Republicans may cease to exist. It is that electoral punishment reportedly failed to produce visible moderation among the officials still controlling the party.

Trump denied responsibility. House Republicans chose Jordan. The party remained organized around grievance, confrontation and loyalty to its leader. Those were decisions made by people with institutional power, not symptoms of collective confusion.

AlterNet weakens that indictment when it substitutes insults and fantasies of annihilation for an exact account of responsibility. Stephen Miller’s elevation is politically significant because of the authority attached to the chief-of-staff position and the agenda he represents; calling him a Nazi without establishing that characterization in the supplied reporting adds heat while sacrificing precision.

Defeat is not disposal

A landslide can interrupt a governing project, transfer offices and expose the limits of a coalition. It cannot permanently settle the political conflict that produced that coalition.

The systemic lesson is harsher than the extinction story. Parties survive catastrophic losses when their donors, media networks, state organizations and officeholders retain incentives to rebuild. If Republican officials continue choosing Trump’s politics after defeat, they own the consequences. If Democrats mistake a wave for permanent realignment, they may surrender the advantage before those consequences arrive.

Political power does not die from embarrassment. It recedes when opponents defeat it repeatedly, dismantle the structures that protect it and govern well enough to make its return less likely.

item.title: Nobody's talking about the real reason behind the biggest landslide since 1964
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet argues that the decisive force behind the reported 2026 Democratic landslide was a broad rejection of authoritarian governance—not any single dispute over war, tariffs, or impeachment. The outlet cites a 13.5-point Democratic lead in the national House vote after more than 116 million votes were counted and a reported gain of 545 state-legislative seats.

The article attributes that coalition to voters reacting to different exercises of institutional power: Hispanic voters to ICE enforcement, Black voters to the Supreme Court’s weakening of the Voting Rights Act, religious liberals to the administration’s use of Christianity, and the No Kings movement to perceived lawlessness generally.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

It also reports that prominent Democrats increasingly refused customary gestures of reconciliation. Governor-elect Amy Acton rejected contact with defeated opponent Vivek Ramaswamy after his campaign used her estranged mother in an advertisement; Hakeem Jeffries called Stephen Miller “a stone-cold racist”; and Representative Stephen Lynch answered a reported White House warning against congressional investigations with, “come at me, bro.”

Power was the issue

The narrowest interpretation of an election is often the safest one for those already holding power. Prices can be adjusted. Tariffs can be revised. Wars can be wound down. But an electorate rejecting the political use of police power, judicial power, racial hierarchy, and executive impunity is rejecting the governing arrangement itself.

That is the article’s strongest argument. The reported coalition was not united by one policy preference. Its members encountered the same administration through different institutions: immigration enforcement, the courts, religious rhetoric, and executive authority. Treating those reactions as unrelated “issues” strips the power relationship out of each one.

The institutional balance is not obscure. The president commands the executive branch. ICE exercises coercive federal authority. The Supreme Court determines the reach of voting protections. Congressional leaders decide whether oversight becomes accountability or ceremony. Voters can punish those institutions electorally, but they do not wield their machinery.

The moderation trap

The strategist quoted by AlterNet compares polling on Iran, tariffs, and impeachment as though Democrats must select one instruction from a menu. That framing converts a sweeping electoral result into tactical advice designed to limit what the winners may do with it.

Impeachment polling does not settle whether Congress should investigate alleged misconduct. Opposition to war or tariffs does not mean voters consented to executive lawlessness everywhere else. Different majorities can reject several abuses at once. The insistence on finding one permissible explanation is not analytical discipline; it is political containment.

The misdirection is aimed downward. Instead of scrutinizing the officials who exercised state power, the argument warns Democrats against responding too forcefully. Responsibility shifts from those who created the conflict to those expected to manage it politely.

Civility for the aggressor

The reported episodes involving Acton, Jeffries, and Lynch expose how “conciliation” can operate as an asymmetric demand. Ramaswamy’s campaign reportedly deployed Acton’s estranged mother despite the history AlterNet describes: Acton said her stepfather raped her when she was 12 and her mother accused her of lying. Asking Acton to restore normal relations afterward would make her conduct—not the campaign’s decision—the test of political decency.

The same structure appears in Jonathan Karl’s questions about whether Jeffries would contact Trump. According to AlterNet, Trump had not called to congratulate Jeffries, yet the burden of reconciliation was placed on Jeffries. The person denied the courtesy was invited to supply it.

Civility becomes institutional cowardice when it requires the target of an abuse to repair the appearance of normal government. It protects the aggressor from consequence while marketing the weaker party’s restraint as statesmanship.

Accountability is not polarization

AlterNet reports that the White House warned congressional Democrats that investigating the administration could itself be criminal. If accurately characterized, that is not ordinary partisan friction. It is an attempt to place executive intimidation between Congress and its oversight power.

The actors and choices are concrete: the administration issued the warning; congressional Democrats must decide whether to retreat; and the press must decide whether to describe the conflict as a struggle over constitutional authority or flatten it into another round of partisan hostility.

Calling racism racist or treating threats against oversight as intimidation does not create the underlying conflict. The conflict was created by the conduct. “Polarization” is frequently the label applied after powerful officials cross a line and their opponents decline to pretend otherwise.

The system rewards selective blindness

The larger pattern is an elite preference for stability of appearance over accountability in practice. Republican escalation is treated as an enduring condition to be accommodated; Democratic resistance is treated as the disruptive choice. That arrangement grants one side agency and assigns the other side responsibility for everyone’s comfort.

AlterNet’s interpretation of the reported landslide is therefore less about Democratic messaging than about whether electoral victory changes institutional behavior. Winning seats matters only if those officials use their authority: investigate executive conduct, defend voting rights, check coercive agencies, and refuse rituals that erase responsibility.

A political system does not correct itself because the injured parties remain gracious. It changes when abuses stop producing compliance and begin producing enforceable consequences.

item.title: The Internet Doesn’t Believe in Rehabilitation
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
We demand that people learn from their mistakes, then spend the rest of their lives reminding them of who they used to be.

Imagine being judged today for the stupidest thing you said when you were fifteen.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Not something you said last week. Not something you still believe. Something you said decades ago, perhaps trying to impress your friends, perhaps repeating something you didn't understand, perhaps simply being an idiot.

You grew up.

You learned.

You changed your mind.

Maybe you even became an outspoken opponent of the very behavior you once engaged in.

None of that matters.

Someone found a screenshot.

And now, apparently, you are fifteen again.

Welcome to the Internet, where your past is permanent, your present is negotiable, and your future can be held hostage by a version of yourself that no longer exists.

We have created a culture that demands personal growth while increasingly refusing to acknowledge that growth is possible.

And somehow, we've convinced ourselves that this represents moral progress.

Your Worst Day Is Now Your Permanent Identity

Human beings have always judged one another.

Gossip didn't begin with Facebook. Public humiliation didn't begin with Twitter. Communities have been ostracizing people for violating social norms since long before anyone invented the printing press.

But there used to be practical limits.

An embarrassing incident might follow you around school. An offensive remark might damage your reputation in your neighborhood. A serious mistake might cost you friendships or professional opportunities.

But time, distance, and changing social circles often provided opportunities to start over.

You could move to another city. Build new relationships. Establish a reputation based on who you had become rather than who you once were.

Not everyone received that opportunity, of course. Social stigma has always been distributed unevenly.

But the possibility existed.

The Internet changed the economics of remembering.

Today, an embarrassing photograph, a tasteless joke, or an angry outburst can be copied, indexed, archived, and circulated indefinitely.

And the Internet has an extraordinary ability to preserve the evidence of someone's worst moments while losing practically everything that might explain them.

Context disappears.

Nuance disappears.

The passage of time becomes irrelevant.

A screenshot from 2008 resurfaces in 2026, accompanied by an accusation written in the present tense.

Not “this person said something offensive eighteen years ago.”

But “look what kind of person this is.”

The past has stopped being evidence of who someone was and become an accusation about who they must still be.

That's not accountability.

That's historical determinism masquerading as moral judgment.

Apparently, Personalities Don't Develop

Here's something peculiar about the way we think.

Nobody expects a forty-year-old to possess the same intellectual abilities they had at fourteen.

We understand that knowledge develops.

Someone who couldn't solve a quadratic equation in high school might become a mathematician.

Someone who struggled with reading as a child might become a successful novelist.

Someone who knew absolutely nothing about programming at sixteen might spend the next twenty years developing software.

We don't consider this remarkable. We call it education.

But apply the same reasoning to moral development, and suddenly things become complicated.

A teenager makes an offensive joke.

Twenty years later, someone discovers it.

And instead of asking whether that person still holds those attitudes, whether their behavior has changed, or whether they've demonstrated a different understanding of the world, the Internet often jumps directly to the verdict.

Guilty.

Not of having said something offensive twenty years ago.

Guilty of being offensive today.

Apparently, intellectual development is perfectly normal, but moral development requires extraordinary proof.

And even that proof might not be enough.

Consider the contradiction.

We teach children about empathy, responsibility, tolerance, and respect precisely because we recognize that those qualities develop over time.

We don't expect children to emerge from the womb with fully formed moral philosophies.

We expect them to make mistakes.

We expect them to learn.

We expect them to become better people.

Then we create digital records of their mistakes and use those records to question whether they ever deserved the opportunity to grow.

We acknowledge that children are unfinished human beings, then preserve their unfinished behavior as though it were their final character assessment.

Accountability Has Become a Life Sentence

In 2025, the Pew Research Center asked American adults whether publicly calling people out on social media for offensive posts was primarily a form of accountability or unjust punishment.

Fifty-six percent considered it accountability. Forty percent saw it primarily as punishing people who didn't deserve it.

The figures reveal a substantial disagreement about what public condemnation actually accomplishes.

And notice the framing.

Accountability or punishment.

As though those concepts were mutually exclusive.

They aren't.

Accountability can involve punishment. Sometimes it should.

But legitimate accountability also requires proportionality, context, and some understanding of what happens after the consequences have been imposed.

Suppose someone makes an offensive remark.

They're confronted.

They acknowledge the remark was wrong.

They apologize.

They educate themselves.

They change their behavior.

Five years pass without another incident.

What happens next?

Under a reasonable understanding of accountability, we might conclude that the intervention worked.

The person learned.

That's supposed to be a good thing.

But under the logic of perpetual online condemnation, the original offense remains available for indefinite prosecution.

The apology becomes irrelevant.

The changed behavior becomes irrelevant.

The passage of time becomes irrelevant.

And if the person objects to being judged for something they did decades ago, that objection itself can be presented as further evidence of their moral deficiency.

Heads, the Internet wins.

Tails, you lose.

This is a system in which no amount of improvement necessarily satisfies the accusation.

And when redemption becomes impossible, accountability has ceased to be corrective.

It has become retribution without an expiration date.

The Internet Doesn't Want Your Explanation. It Wants Your Confession.

There's another disturbing feature of public online controversies.

The demand for an apology often arrives before anyone has established whether the accusation is accurate, complete, or fairly contextualized.

A short clip circulates.

A screenshot appears.

An old statement is rediscovered.

And thousands of strangers begin demanding an explanation from someone they've never met.

The accused person now faces a peculiar dilemma.

Remain silent, and the silence may be interpreted as guilt.

Offer an explanation, and it may be dismissed as making excuses.

Apologize, and the apology may be treated as confirmation of the worst possible interpretation.

Apologize too quickly, and it appears insincere.

Wait too long, and it becomes evidence that the person only regrets getting caught.

There is no universally accepted procedure for demonstrating genuine remorse.

More importantly, there is no universally accepted standard for determining when someone has made sufficient amends.

The audience changes. The accusations evolve. New participants arrive without knowing what has already been addressed.

And every new wave can restart the trial.

The original incident might be fifteen years old.

For someone encountering it for the first time this morning, however, the outrage is brand new.

That's one of the Internet's strangest distortions of time.

An old offense can generate fresh outrage indefinitely, while an old apology rarely enjoys the same circulation.

The Algorithm Has No Interest in Your Redemption

Of course, there is a technological component to all of this.

Social media platforms don't generally distribute content according to its moral value.

Their ranking systems are designed around various objectives, including engagement, relevance, and the likelihood that users will interact with particular material.

And outrage is excellent at attracting attention.

A shocking video invites comments.

An offensive screenshot invites condemnation.

A controversial statement invites arguments.

Arguments generate more comments.

More comments can generate more visibility.

The cycle feeds itself.

Compare that with a different story.

A man made a racist joke at seventeen.

He eventually recognized how offensive it was.

Over the next twenty years, he matured, treated people decently, raised a family, worked with people from different backgrounds, and never repeated the behavior.

Where's the viral content?

There probably isn't any.

Not because his development is unimportant, but because two decades of ordinary, responsible behavior don't fit neatly into a fifteen-second video.

The original offensive remark does.

And that's the structural imbalance.

Misconduct is an event. Personal growth is a process.

Events are easy to record.

Processes are harder to package.

The result is an enormous imbalance between the visibility of someone's mistakes and the visibility of everything they've done since.

A platform doesn't need to deliberately oppose rehabilitation to contribute to that imbalance.

It only needs to reward the material that provokes the strongest reactions.

Even the Law Recognizes That People Can Change

What's particularly ironic is that formal justice systems, for all their considerable flaws, frequently recognize principles that online public judgment ignores.

Many legal systems distinguish between juveniles and adults.

They recognize mitigating circumstances.

They provide for rehabilitation.

They sometimes allow criminal records to be sealed or expunged.

Punishments are generally supposed to have defined limits.

None of these protections is universal, and serious offenses can appropriately have lasting consequences.

But the underlying idea is important.

A human being should not necessarily remain defined forever by a past offense.

Even someone convicted of a crime may eventually complete their sentence and become eligible for reintegration into society.

Yet someone who said something offensive on social media fifteen years ago can remain the subject of recurring public condemnation without any comparable mechanism for closure.

The European Union has attempted to address part of the broader digital problem through the General Data Protection Regulation.

Under certain circumstances, individuals can request the erasure of personal information that is no longer necessary or has been processed unlawfully.

The so-called “right to be forgotten” is not absolute. It includes exceptions for freedom of expression, legal obligations, and other legitimate interests.

Nor does it guarantee that every copy of embarrassing information will disappear.

But the principle is significant.

It acknowledges that permanent digital accessibility is not automatically justified simply because information once became public.

In other words, at least some legal frameworks recognize what online culture frequently overlooks:

The fact that something happened does not mean it must remain equally relevant forever.

No, This Isn't a Demand to Forget Everything

Before anyone reaches for the inevitable accusation, let's establish something.

This is not an argument that people should escape responsibility for their actions.

Nor is it an argument that victims must forgive their abusers.

Some conduct is so serious that it legitimately affects how we evaluate someone's trustworthiness for years afterward.

A history of financial fraud may be relevant when someone applies for a position managing other people's money.

A documented pattern of harassment may be relevant when considering whether someone should supervise vulnerable employees.

And someone who continues repeating the same harmful behavior has not demonstrated meaningful change merely because they issued an apology.

Those distinctions matter.

But so does the distinction between an isolated mistake and a persistent pattern.

Between a teenager's stupidity and an adult's considered beliefs.

Between someone who apologized because they were caught and someone whose subsequent behavior demonstrates that they've genuinely changed.

Between protecting potential victims and simply enjoying the spectacle of condemnation.

The question shouldn't be whether the past can ever matter.

Of course it can.

The question should be how much weight the past deserves when evaluating the present.

And the answer cannot reasonably be “all of it, forever.”

What Happens When Changing Doesn't Matter?

There is a practical problem with creating a culture that refuses to recognize rehabilitation.

It undermines one of the incentives for genuine improvement.

Think about how we encourage people to change.

We tell them to acknowledge their mistakes.

Accept responsibility.

Make amends.

Learn.

Do better.

But what happens when someone does all those things and discovers that the social verdict never changes?

What message are we sending?

Not that mistakes have consequences.

That's a lesson worth teaching.

We're sending the message that mistakes define identity permanently, regardless of what happens afterward.

That's a very different proposition.

A person who believes that improvement can restore trust has a reason to make that improvement visible and sustained.

A person who believes that nothing will ever restore trust may instead become defensive, resentful, or simply disengaged.

This doesn't mean everyone will react that way.

People can and do change for reasons entirely independent of public approval.

But a system that recognizes no meaningful difference between continued misconduct and demonstrated reform is a remarkably poor system for encouraging reform.

It treats the person who keeps doing wrong and the person who stopped doing wrong as morally interchangeable.

And then congratulates itself on maintaining high standards.

We Are All Former Versions of Ourselves

Here's an uncomfortable exercise.

Think about who you were ten years ago.

Think about your opinions, assumptions, habits, prejudices, and beliefs.

Now go back twenty years.

Thirty, if you're old enough.

Would you agree with everything that earlier version of yourself believed?

Would you defend every joke?

Every argument?

Every decision?

Would you want every angry conversation, every immature remark, and every moment of spectacular stupidity preserved for strangers to inspect?

Most people wouldn't.

Because most people recognize that they've changed.

And that's perfectly normal.

In fact, it's desirable.

We should be worried about someone who has learned absolutely nothing from decades of experience.

Yet there's an extraordinary asymmetry in how we approach this.

We freely recognize our own personal growth.

We explain our old mistakes in terms of youth, ignorance, circumstance, and lessons learned.

But when evaluating strangers, especially strangers encountered through viral controversy, we often become far less generous.

Their mistakes reveal character.

Ours reflect circumstances.

Their apologies are suspicious.

Ours are sincere.

Their past defines them.

Ours explains how far we've come.

It's remarkable how easily the principle of human complexity disappears when the human being in question is someone we don't know.

The Difference Between Remembering and Understanding

The Internet's greatest achievement may also be one of its greatest social liabilities.

It remembers.

An astonishing amount of human activity can now be preserved and retrieved.

Statements that would once have disappeared into the air remain available years later.

Photographs survive.

Videos survive.

Arguments survive.

And there's considerable value in that.

Digital records have exposed corruption, documented abuses, preserved history, and helped hold powerful people accountable.

We shouldn't pretend otherwise.

But memory and understanding are not the same thing.

A photograph tells us what someone looked like at a particular moment.

It doesn't tell us everything about their life.

A video records behavior.

It doesn't necessarily explain the circumstances surrounding it.

A twenty-year-old statement reveals something about what a person said twenty years ago.

It does not automatically establish what that person believes today.

Yet our online culture frequently treats these fragments as complete biographies.

We have access to more information about other people than ever before.

And we sometimes use that information to make remarkably shallow judgments.

The Internet has become extraordinarily good at remembering what people did, and remarkably bad at recognizing who they've become.

Rehabilitation Requires a Future

Ultimately, this isn't just about embarrassing photographs or offensive jokes.

It's about what kind of society we want to build.

One in which mistakes have consequences, but people have opportunities to learn from them?

Or one in which a sufficiently public mistake becomes a permanent label, regardless of subsequent behavior?

A society that genuinely values accountability must also value the possibility of successful accountability.

Otherwise, what exactly are we trying to accomplish?

If someone acknowledges wrongdoing, makes amends, changes their behavior, and demonstrates that change over time, shouldn't that count for something?

Not necessarily automatic forgiveness.

Not immunity from criticism.

Not an obligation for anyone to trust them.

But something.

There should be a meaningful distinction between the person who made a mistake and learned from it and the person who continues making the same mistake without remorse.

Without that distinction, moral judgment becomes little more than historical bookkeeping.

A ledger of offenses, continuously updated, with no mechanism for recognizing improvement.

And that's a terrible model of human development.

Because people are not static objects.

They're not photographs.

They're not screenshots.

They're not fifteen-second video clips.

They're complicated, changing human beings, capable of ignorance and understanding, cruelty and kindness, failure and improvement.

Sometimes they become worse.

Sometimes they become better.

And sometimes the person they were twenty years ago would barely recognize the person they've become.

A society that claims to believe in personal growth has to allow people to outgrow their past.

Otherwise, we're not encouraging people to become better.

We're merely demanding that they have always been perfect.

And nobody qualifies.

Systemic Error — The failure was designed.

Sources and further reading

  • Pew Research Center — “In a shift, more Republicans now say calling people out on social media represents accountability” (October 15, 2025)

  • Pew Research Center — “Americans and ‘Cancel Culture’: Where Some See Calls for Accountability, Others See Censorship, Punishment” (May 19, 2021)

  • European Commission — GDPR rights and the right to erasure

item.content:encoded:
When a father turned his son's bullying punishment into viral content, he may have created consequences that will outlive the lesson.

A father in Spokane, Washington, recently discovered that his thirteen-year-old son had been bullying children smaller than himself.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

According to the father's account, his son had intimidated another boy and told a girl that she should kill herself.

Let's establish something immediately: this wasn't harmless childhood mischief. Telling another child to take her own life is vicious behavior, and any responsible parent discovering something like this should take it seriously.

This father certainly did.

The man, a content creator who goes by Boosted Speed Demon on TikTok, decided to teach his son what it feels like to be physically intimidated by someone bigger and stronger.

The father stands six feet four inches tall and weighs approximately 220 pounds. His thirteen-year-old son is already five feet ten and weighs 160 pounds.

The boy was accustomed to having a considerable physical advantage over his victims. His father decided to reverse that equation.

He put boxing gloves and protective headgear on his son, put on his own gloves, and confronted him. He challenged the boy to fight, repeatedly demanded that he throw punches, and eventually struck him twice.

The frightened teenager cried, said he didn't want to be a bully, and promised not to bully anyone again.

The father subsequently required his son to write apology letters to the children he'd allegedly bullied. He also said he would include his own phone number so their parents could contact him directly if the behavior continued.

The Internet exploded.

Some viewers applauded the father for refusing to tolerate bullying. Others condemned his methods as abusive.

But amid the arguments over corporal punishment, tough love, and whether the father had gone too far, another decision deserves scrutiny.

He recorded the punishment and published it on the Internet.

And that may prove to be the most consequential decision he made.

Discipline Is Supposed to Have an Ending

Parents have been debating appropriate disciplinary methods for as long as there have been parents.

Some believe physical punishment is never acceptable. Others believe that a sufficiently serious offense may warrant an immediate, memorable physical consequence.

There is considerable disagreement about where discipline ends and abuse begins, and research raises substantial concerns about the harms associated with corporal punishment.

We don't need to resolve that entire debate to examine what happened here.

For the sake of argument, suppose the father achieved exactly what he intended.

Suppose his son genuinely understood the fear he had been inflicting on smaller children. Suppose the experience awakened his empathy, changed his behavior, and ensured that he never bullied anyone again.

Suppose, in other words, that the punishment worked.

Why, then, should the boy still be paying for it ten years from now?

Because that's the possibility his father introduced when he uploaded the video.

Traditional discipline, whatever its form, generally has a beginning and an end.

A child misbehaves. A parent intervenes. There are consequences. Ideally, the child learns something, makes amends, and moves forward.

The incident becomes part of the child's development, not a permanent public identity.

But social media changes that equation.

A punishment that might have lasted a few minutes becomes a video that can circulate indefinitely.

And the child loses control over who sees it, how it is interpreted, and when it might resurface.

Imagine the Job Interview

Fast-forward ten years.

The boy is now twenty-three.

Perhaps he's finished college. Perhaps he's applying for his first serious job. Perhaps he's become a responsible, compassionate young man who would be horrified by the way he behaved at thirteen.

An employer searches his name.

And there it is.

A video of him being confronted by his father over bullying smaller children, including a girl he allegedly told to kill herself.

The recruiter doesn't know the man sitting across the desk.

Not really.

They don't know whether he learned his lesson. They don't know how he behaved throughout high school. They don't know whether he became an advocate against bullying, helped other children, or spent the intervening decade being a thoroughly decent human being.

They know what happened one afternoon when he was thirteen.

And they have video.

Of course, the video isn't guaranteed to appear in an employer's search. That depends on how widely it circulates, whether the boy is identifiable, and how easily it can be connected to his adult identity.

But once the footage is public, those possibilities are no longer entirely within the family's control.

The father has effectively created a record that could follow his son into adulthood.

Not because the boy committed some offense requiring a permanent public record.

Not because a court determined that society needed to be warned about him.

But because his father decided that his punishment belonged on TikTok.

Accountability Is Not Entertainment

There's something else about this story that deserves attention.

The father is a content creator.

His TikTok account ordinarily features automotive content. This time, he published a deeply personal disciplinary confrontation involving his own child.

According to reporting by The Mary Sue, the video accumulated more than three million likes.

That's an extraordinary amount of engagement.

And it raises an uncomfortable question.

When does documenting parental discipline become turning a child's humiliation into content?

I'm not suggesting that the father invented the incident for views, or that online attention was his primary motivation. We have no evidence establishing either claim.

His anger at discovering his son's behavior may have been entirely genuine. His disciplinary intentions may have been sincere.

But intentions do not erase consequences.

Social media rewards emotionally charged material. Confrontations, tears, humiliation, and dramatic moral lessons are exceptionally effective at generating engagement.

And children provide a particularly troubling source of content because they generally lack the power to refuse participation.

A thirteen-year-old cannot reasonably be expected to understand the long-term implications of becoming the subject of a viral video.

He cannot meaningfully negotiate how that footage will be distributed.

He cannot ensure that copies are deleted.

And he cannot predict how strangers might interpret it a decade later.

His father, however, is an adult.

He should understand that publishing something and controlling it are two very different things.

The audience may applaud today and forget tomorrow.

The child may not have that luxury.

The Victims Still Matter

None of this should distract from the children who were allegedly bullied.

They deserve protection, acknowledgment, and appropriate intervention.

The girl who was reportedly told to kill herself deserves particular attention. Statements like that cannot be dismissed as ordinary teasing, and ensuring her well-being should be a priority.

The father's decision to require apology letters was a constructive element of his response.

So was his willingness to make himself available to the victims' families.

Those actions establish something more important than a public spectacle: responsibility.

They communicate that bullying is unacceptable, that the harm done to others matters, and that the offender must take steps toward making things right.

The letters also create an opportunity for the son to confront what he actually did.

He has to acknowledge his behavior, consider its effects, and express remorse.

Whether his apologies are sincere, and whether his behavior changes, can only be determined over time.

But that's how accountability is supposed to work.

The objective shouldn't merely be to make a child suffer for doing something wrong.

It should be to help ensure that the child stops doing it.

And nothing about that objective requires an audience of millions.

A Child Is Not a Finished Product

This is the part we seem increasingly willing to forget.

The boy is thirteen.

His behavior, as described by his father, was reprehensible.

But a thirteen-year-old is not a finished human being.

Children are still developing emotionally, intellectually, and morally. They are learning empathy, impulse control, responsibility, and the relationship between their actions and other people's suffering.

That's one of the fundamental reasons we treat children differently from adults.

We recognize that immaturity matters.

We recognize that judgment develops.

And, perhaps most importantly, we recognize that children can change.

Imagine applying the same standard to intellectual development that we increasingly apply to moral development.

Imagine someone being denied an engineering job at thirty because a video surfaced of them struggling with fractions at thirteen.

It would be absurd.

We understand that mathematical knowledge develops through education and experience.

Why are we sometimes so reluctant to extend that same understanding to character?

A child who behaves cruelly at thirteen may become a cruel adult.

Or he may become someone profoundly ashamed of that behavior, precisely because he eventually develops the empathy he once lacked.

The distinction matters.

And a permanent digital record of childhood misconduct can make it harder for others to recognize that distinction.

The Father May Have Won the Battle and Lost the War

There is a cruel irony in all this.

The father wanted to teach his son that actions have consequences.

That's a legitimate lesson.

But by publishing the punishment, he introduced consequences that may be far beyond anything the boy could have anticipated.

Consequences that may continue long after the original wrongdoing has been acknowledged, addressed, and corrected.

And consequences that the father himself may be unable to reverse.

He could have confronted his son privately.

He could have required the apology letters.

He could have contacted the school and the victims' parents.

He could have monitored his son's behavior and made clear that further bullying would bring serious consequences.

All without involving millions of strangers.

Instead, he made his son's misconduct — and his punishment — a public event.

It's possible that the boy will never experience any lasting harm from the video. Perhaps it will fade into digital obscurity, never to resurface in any consequential way.

I hope that's what happens.

But hope isn't a particularly sound strategy for protecting a child's future.

Especially when the risk was entirely avoidable.

The Right to Become Someone Better

Parents are supposed to prepare their children for adulthood.

That means teaching them responsibility, empathy, and consequences.

It also means protecting their opportunities to grow beyond their mistakes.

A child who does something terrible should face appropriate consequences.

But those consequences should serve a purpose.

They should help correct behavior, encourage understanding, protect victims, and create an opportunity for improvement.

They shouldn't become an indelible public label.

There is a profound difference between teaching a child that wrongdoing has consequences and ensuring that wrongdoing becomes part of his permanent identity.

The first is a responsibility of parenting.

The second can become an obstacle to everything parenting is supposed to accomplish.

Perhaps this boy will grow into a wonderful adult.

Perhaps he'll look back on that afternoon as the moment he finally understood why bullying was wrong.

Perhaps he'll even thank his father for intervening.

But he should also have the opportunity to leave that afternoon behind.

Because the purpose of raising children is not to preserve evidence of everything they did wrong. It's to help them become adults who know how to do better.

And the Internet doesn't need a front-row seat to that process.

Source: Vanessa Esguerra, “Washington dad discovers his son is bullying smaller kids. He decided to teach his son a harsh lesson,” The Mary Sue, November 10, 2026.

item.title: GOP lawmaker turns on Trump’s war in fiery MAGA TV appearance
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened Rep. Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican who initially supported President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, now calls it “terrible policy.” AlterNet reports that Harrigan blamed the conflict’s economic fallout—particularly higher gas prices—for Republicans’ midterm losses and his own narrow reelection.
